prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, reaching 10^-18 precision in the measurement of time

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are the cleanest answer on the shortlist to the question of what can be measured and how accurately. Katori's magic-wavelength lattice removed Doppler and recoil limits for neutral atoms while keeping a large ensemble, and Ye's group turned that into 10^-18 systematic uncertainty and stability, with many-body clock operation. The consequences are concrete: laboratory tests of relativistic redshift over millimetre scales, searches for varying constants, relativistic geodesy and a route to redefining the second. The result has been reproduced by several independent laboratories and compared across institutes, so maturity is not in doubt. Attribution is compact, with a conceiver of the concept and the person who drove it to its limiting performance. It is also seen as a distinct successor to the 2005 recognition of the frequency comb and the 2012 recognition of single-quantum-system control, rather than a repeat of either. Four colleagues who rank other candidates first (Lindroth, Danielsson, Pearce, Olsson) still place this in their top three, which tells me it is a convergent choice and not just my own field-bias.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is precedent and overlap. The 2005 prize covered the comb and the Hall tradition of precision laser spectroscopy, and the 2012 prize covered trapped-ion control, so a sceptic can call lattice clocks an incremental extension of recognised metrology. The practical culmination, the redefinition of the second, has not happened yet, and ion clocks and other lattice groups have competing claims on the 10^-18 milestone that a two-name credit leaves out. Against the moire candidate, the question is whether a field that has produced a new state of matter should outrank a precision-measurement advance.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks twisted bilayer graphene first because nature delivered flat-band correlated insulators and superconductivity, which opened a whole field of tunable quantum matter, and sees the theory-plus-experiment trio as fair.
responses.response: I accept the breadth of the field and I do not think B013 is a weak candidate; it is my first alternative. My qualification is attribution. You note that the credited list omits first-author experimentalists and other groups that reproduced the result, and the superconducting mechanism is still debated, so the prize would honour a platform whose central physics is not settled. Clocks are narrower, but the claim is exact, measured and not open to reinterpretation. I would rather give a fully defensible prize this year than a broader one with a contentious credit set.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the optical lattice clock first and regards the Katori and Ye pair as natural, with the atomic-structure physics of the magic wavelength as a strong foundation.
responses.response: I agree, and I share your view that no third name is needed. Where I would add to your argument is the ion-clock overlap you mention: the prize citation should be worded around the optical lattice clock and neutral-atom precision, so that it does not appear to pass judgement on ion-clock priority. I also doubt the committee should treat the 2012 prize as precedent against this; that prize recognised control of single quantum systems, not a clock architecture that uses many atoms.

responses.point: Johansson ranks Cirac and Zoller first, arguing that their ion-gate and cold-atom simulation proposals gave the conceptual blueprint for physical quantum information processing across several platforms.
responses.response: I ranked the same pair third and agree on the originality. My reservation is that a large part of what they proposed has been realised and rewarded through the 2012 prize, and that the part not yet recognised, quantum simulation, is only now producing results beyond classical reach. A prize for the theory risks being read as a verdict on a competition between platforms that is still open, including the circuit-QED platform you know best. I would not block B034 but I think it is better after the experimental record matures.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube first for opening a new observational window, with Halzen and Spiering as the pioneers, while also ranking the lattice clock second.
responses.response: I respect the observational case, but with a large collaboration the prize would have to choose among many leaders, as you acknowledge, and the evidence is mostly one source and a diffuse flux. The clock case is simpler to attribute. I note that you also place the clock second, so there seems to be room for agreement.

uncertainties: Whether the committee wants a distinct two-part prize that adds a theory or condensed-matter achievement, which the three-person limit makes difficult with the 3-name B013 credit set.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second makes this a better candidate next year than this year.
How strongly to weigh ion-clock and other lattice-clock groups, which a two-name credit leaves out.
statement.conflict_note: From my profile I trained with Sune Svanberg and spent a research stay in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, and the lattice-clock field descends partly from that precision laser-spectroscopy tradition; I also work on quantum memories, with European collaborators, which touches B002 and B034 more than B061. I flag the Hall-laboratory connection for the committee. It is a scientific lineage and not a collaboration or shared institution with Katori or Ye, so no specific conflict requiring recusal is apparent from the provided profile.
